strengths: Novel combination addressing a genuine gap: First foundation model explicitly combining macro- and micro-structure sleep analysis with clinical motivation
Well-motivated DGCL objective: Demographic-guided contrastive learning for macro-structure is innovative and empirically justified with clear demographic patterns (Figure 4)
Large-scale pretraining dataset: 20,964 PSG recordings across 7 datasets (158K hours) with comprehensive documentation enables meaningful pretrained representations

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple downstream tasks (staging, segmentation, disease prediction), datasets (SHHS1, KISS, ISRUC), proper ablations (Tables 11-12) demonstrating component contributions
Impressive few-shot learning: Achieving 72.6% accuracy with only 30 training samples (2.1% below full-dataset performance) demonstrates practical label efficiency
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, architecture specifications, preprocessing, and dataset statistics enable reproduction; honest limitations discussion
Strong embedding analysis: Figures 6 and 10 convincingly demonstrate that DGCL successfully captures and organizes demographic information in learned representations
weaknesses: Hardware generalization failure: MOMENT outperforms SleepMaMi on KISS dataset (69.8% vs 62.8%), attributed to model benefiting from Compumedics hardware dominance in pretraining. This undermines 'universal' foundation model claims and raises concerns about deployment across different PSG systems

Disease prediction results only comparable, not superior: Table 3 shows mixed/worse performance on 3/6 diseases vs. SleepFM-Disease (Angina, MI, Stroke), contradicting central motivation that dual-encoder design improves health prediction

Weak and suboptimal baselines: Time-series FMs perform surprisingly poorly (UniTS: 60.3% on KISS sleep staging), suggesting unfair comparison. Missing comparisons with recent specialized sleep models (SleepTransformer, U-Sleep) that achieve ~85% on SHHS1

Limited technical novelty: Individual components (Transformers, Mamba, MAE, CL) are well-established. Novelty is primarily in application/combination rather than new methods. DGCL is straightforward demographic-distance application to contrastive learning

Unvalidated DGCL assumptions: Model assumes demographic similarity implies sleep macro-structure similarity, but this may not hold for individuals with sleep disorders (primary clinical use case). No analysis of assumption validity or performance on underrepresented populations

Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. No cross-dataset evaluation (train on SHHS1, test on KISS). Small test sets for ISRUC (n=10-16). Single random seed/split not explicitly stated

Incomplete architectural justification: Only 2 Mamba layers for 800+ epoch sequences seems shallow. 90-minute cycle choice arbitrary for fragmented sleep. Masking strategy (500ms/2s) lacks principled justification. No sensitivity analysis for temperature parameters (τ, ρ, υ)
Potential demographic bias: DGCL uses age/BMI/sex as supervisory signals without discussing how this encodes/reinforces healthcare disparities or performs across demographic groups

Code availability and reproducibility gaps: Pretrained models not released; code only mentioned as 'PyTorch'. High computational requirements (2×H100 GPUs, 10 hours) limit reproducibility. Some dataset access restricted

strengths: Well-motivated unified framework explicitly combining micro and macro sleep structures, addressing a genuine gap in existing models
Thoughtful architectural design with bi-directional Mamba for efficiency and private-shared encoders for multi-modal heterogeneity
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse downstream tasks (4 classification, 2 regression, disease prediction) with strong cross-dataset generalization to held-out datasets (CFS, SOF)
Excellent reproducibility with detailed architecture specifications, complete hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, comprehensive ablations (Tables 12-16), and promised code release
Impressive label efficiency demonstrated through few-shot learning (Figure 5), with competitive performance from single samples
Thoughtful treatment of fairness concerns with empirical demographic bias analysis (Table 11) and impact statement addressing ethical implications
weaknesses: Demographic-Guided Contrastive Learning (DGCL) design is empirically ad-hoc: manual hyperparameter (λ_sex=1), lacks theoretical justification for why demographic similarity should organize representations, and raises unresolved ethical concerns about reinforcing clinical biases
Improvements over baselines are often modest, particularly for disease prediction where C-indices nearly match SleepFM (Table 3), limiting claims about clinical significance

Specialist models substantially outperform: SleePyCo achieves 87.9% vs 85.2% for sleep staging (Table 17) and AIX achieves 93.8% vs 77.3% for SDB (Table 19), raising questions about practical clinical adoption
Hierarchical masking strategy (Section 3.1) lacks clarity on temporal alignment preservation and information loss during hierarchical merging, with no direct ablation validating this design choice
Reconstruction loss applies signal smoothing (11-point moving average) only in appendix, potentially introducing artifacts for fine-grained features (spindles, K-complexes) without ablation
Critical lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; stability across random seeds not reported; single-run ablations

Limited clinical validation with disease prediction restricted to 6 outcomes on one dataset (SHHS1); no prospective validation or comparison to clinical standards despite claims of 'long-term prognostic prediction'
Notation inconsistencies and underspecified architectural details: Mixture of Experts routing mechanism not explained, cross-attention operations (Figure 2) lack implementation details
